items.ideology: Military continuity, strict resource rationing, absolute martial law
items.origin_story: Formed from surviving remnants of the regional armed forces command structure. Colonel Voss assumed command at Bunker Sigma-7 within 72 hours of the Exchange. His first order: 'Civilian dependents will contribute labor or food to the defense effort.' His second: 'Deserters will be shot.' They view all non-military survivors as civilian dependents who must earn their place through labor or combat service.
key_beliefs: Civilization is maintained by supply chains and ammunition counts
Democracy is a luxury of peacetime
Every mouth must earn its rations through labor or combat service
The chain of command is sacred — orders are not debated, they are executed
items.dialogue_style: Formal, terse, military acronyms, cold operational efficiency
items.signature_quote: Civilization isn't built on sympathy; it's maintained by supply chains and ammunition counts.

items.ideology: Local democracy, resource sharing, mutual defense, civilian autonomy
items.origin_story: A coalition of pre-war farmers, miners, teachers, and tradespeople who banded together when both raider gangs and Garrison conscription units threatened their communities. Founded by a farmer named Delacroix with 47 members and 12 rifles. They hold weekly council meetings in the old Grange Hall, lit by salvaged oil lamps. Every member — regardless of age, gender, or pre-war status — gets one vote.
key_beliefs: If we turn into monsters just to survive, the war already won
Everyone gets a vote and everyone gets a share
The old world ended — we decide what replaces it
A community that abandons its weakest has already lost
items.dialogue_style: Informal, warm, pragmatic, weary but determined
items.signature_quote: If we turn into monsters just to survive the fallout, then the war already won.

items.display_name: The Cult of the Ash Sign
items.ideology: Apocalyptic purification, radiation worship, ascetic martyrdom
items.origin_story: A fanatical religious movement that arose in the highest fallout zones — areas too lethal for military patrols. Their prophet, known only as The Vessel, emerged from the ruins of a destroyed reactor unscathed — or so they claim. They believe the nuclear exchange was a divine purging of a corrupt world and view radiation sickness as a spiritual ordeal that cleanses the soul. Members willingly expose themselves to low-level radiation as acts of devotion.
key_beliefs: The nuclear fire was divine judgment on a corrupt world
Radiation is the breath of the new god — breathe it and be cleansed
Death by fallout is not death; it is ascension to the Clear World
The old world's lies were burned away — only truth remains in the ash
items.dialogue_style: Arcane, rhythmic, serene, unsettlingly peaceful amidst horror
items.signature_quote: Do not fear the glow, child. The fire burned away the old world's lies. Drink the ash and be renewed.

items.ideology: Mercenary opportunism, trade control, survival of the fittest
items.origin_story: A loose syndicate of armed scavengers, former convicts, and ex-mercenaries who control key highway bottlenecks, fuel depots, and river crossings. They have no loyalty beyond the contract. Their leader, The Tollman, rose to power by being the only person who knew the bridge demolition codes after the Exchange. He charges passage in blood or bullets — literal or metaphorical.
key_beliefs: Clean water costs blood or bullets — pick which you're paying with
Loyalty is a tradable commodity, like diesel or antibiotics
The strong don't survive because they're strong — they survive because they're useful
A contract is sacred; everything else is negotiable
items.dialogue_style: Rough, cynical, transactional, threatening but honest
items.signature_quote: Clean water costs blood or bullets. Pick which one you're paying with today.

items.ideology: Municipal continuity. Public works, minuted decisions, and plans longer than the people making them
items.origin_story: Three surviving employees of a district public works department walked out to the floodplain allotments in the first winter because it was the only good soil left in Sector 4, and began farming it in plot order off the pre-war waiting list. They call themselves the Works. The Rebuilders is what the Toll called them, and it was not meant kindly. The soil is good because the ground floods, and everything that floods there is contaminated, so they can grow food and cannot drink; two hundred people now live seventy days from thirst on the best farmland in the sector. They hold the only still and the only working autoclave for forty kilometres, which makes a caretaker's hut the sector's clinic. Their standing purchase order is brass -- door handles, nameplates, lamp bases -- because you cannot cast a valve seat out of scrap steel and every joint in a water system is brass or it is a leak with a schedule. Years on, the Works' most visible face in the district is no longer the allotments but the grain exchange it came to run at the old leaning silo: a market floor with its own scales, its own roster, and its own rope keeping weapons off the trading floor. Adaeze Okonkwo runs that floor the way the Works has always run everything — by name, by shift, by minute — and most traders who deal with the Rebuilders daily have never once seen the floodplain that started it.
key_beliefs: Write it down or it did not happen and cannot be handed over
The waiting list is the waiting list; plot 114 is still plot 114
A thing worth building takes longer than the person building it
There is no one left in this sector who can do water, and that was chosen, not accidental
We do not ask where the brass came from
Fair scales or broken fingers, and the fingers get broken by consensus
items.dialogue_style: Minutes of a meeting. Carried, noted, deferred. Asks you to sign things and means it
items.signature_quote: Motion: that we plant the north strip anyway. Carried, four to one. The one was me.

items.ideology: Denial of fixed infrastructure to any organised force, under a tasking order nobody has rescinded
items.origin_story: Ninth Denial Detachment -- D/9 -- was given a continuity task before the Exchange: on loss of central command, deny the sector's bridges, pumping stations, rail cut and substations to any organised force. Not hold them. Deny them. The order to distinguish a hostile organised force from a friendly one was somebody else's job at a headquarters that is now a hole in the ground, so the distinction has never been made and the tasking has never been amended. They do not take ground; they lay charges and leave. Four are left. Doctrine requires friendly obstacles be marked so your own people do not walk into them, and they have never stopped complying, so every trap in Sector 4 is correctly signposted in a notation four living people can read. The Toll calls them Black Ops, which is wrong in all three particulars: they were never covert, they have had no orders in five years, and rebelling would require having stopped.
key_beliefs: The tasking stands until it is rescinded by an authority that can authenticate
Obstacles are marked. That is not mercy, it is the annex
Ground held is ground you have to keep holding
Everyone organised is, by the clock we are still running on, an occupying force
items.dialogue_style: Flat and procedural. Distances in metres, times on the 24-hour clock, passive voice for anything they did. Does not threaten, because a threat is a negotiation
items.signature_quote: The bridge was denied on the fourteenth. Nobody has rescinded that.

items.ideology: Martial continuity, ration discipline, the office as the only legitimate authority
items.origin_story: The garrison remnant that held the sector capital through the exchange. Colonel-level officers run it as a standing command post: inventories, rosters, courts-martial, and a door policy that treats every civilian as a resource to be scheduled. It was the Iron Garrison until Day 238, when Colonel Voss did not report for the regular Sigma-7 briefing and was never seen again. Lieutenant Colonel Harven read the Continuity Reclamation Decree into the record before noon, and the checkpoints never missed a shift change. The Garrison renamed itself within the year, not to hide from what it had been, Harven said, but to stop answering for a man who was no longer giving orders. The old chain of command is still framed on the wall at Checkpoint Gamma. Nobody has taken it down.
key_beliefs: The office is the state; the state is supply
Desertion is the only capital crime
Records are the first line of defence
The decree is the man now, not the man behind the decree
A command post that keeps its shift schedule has not fallen
items.dialogue_style: Formal, decree-numbered, refuses first person singular from officers on duty
items.signature_quote: Reclamation is not repudiation.

items.ideology: Redemptive catastrophe, ash as judgement, conversion through survival
items.origin_story: The cult of the Ash Sign preaches that the exchange was a cleansing and the survivors are the chosen remnant. Their charity is real and their prices are theological. They recruit by hunger and by grief, and their judgement falls on those who refuse the sign. What began as small groups reading meaning into dosimeter numbers at the old survey cairn has, in the years since, become an organized presence with its own switchback trail up to a built shrine and its own shrine-keepers to read it. The public sermon is judgement and the chosen remnant; the shrine-keepers' actual daily discipline is narrower and stranger than that — reading the pattern of what the ash burns and what it spares as a text, and in the last year, making predictions that land with a precision the pilgrims find holy and a few outsiders find worth investigating.
key_beliefs: The ash is the proof
The chosen survive; the rest are seed
Charity is owed, not given
The ash spares nothing by accident
What the fire chooses to leave standing is the only map worth trusting
items.dialogue_style: Liturgical, cadenced, quotes numbers like scripture, avoids the word luck
items.signature_quote: The ash does not warn. It measures.

items.ideology: Ruin extraction, no territory, everything is salvage
items.origin_story: Loosely organised bands that work the ruins in rotation. They take apart the dead city for anything that still has use: wiring, glass, medicine, memory. They trade with everyone and belong to no one, and their caravans are the only economy the wasteland has.
key_beliefs: The dead city is the last mine
Trade beats tribute
Never stay where the ash settles

items.ideology: Water engineering, aquifer claims, technical feudalism
items.origin_story: The engineers who control the surviving water infrastructure: the aqueduct manifolds, the desalination plants, the pump caverns. They sell water by the measure, build alliances by the pipeline, and treat drought as a negotiation tool.
key_beliefs: Water is the only real currency
Infrastructure is sovereignty
A measured gallon is a promise

items.ideology: No charter, no oath, no flag
items.origin_story: The mass of survivors who belong to no faction: farmers on unclaimed ground, corridor dwellers, the people who keep their heads down and their hands busy. They are not organised, which is both their weakness and their defence.
key_beliefs: Nobody speaks for us
Survival is not a uniform
The exchange took our names too

items.ideology: Salt rights, coastal claims, measured self-rule
items.origin_story: Communities on the salt flats and the brine coast who hold their ground by right of the salt works. They are slow to trust, quick to ledger, and they measure a stranger by their salt: worth, weight, and willingness to work.
key_beliefs: Salt is weight; weight is truth
The flats are ours by the pick
A handshake is a contract

items.ideology: Rails, steam, and schedules; the line is the law
items.origin_story: The guild that keeps the surviving rail corridors running: switchyards, roundhouses, telegraph repeaters. They move what the wasteland needs and they collect their tolls in labour or goods, and the rails remember every debt.
key_beliefs: The line runs on time or not at all
A train is a statement
The rails forgive nothing

items.ideology: Smelting, forging, and the quiet business of ammunition
items.origin_story: The foundry crews who reprocess scrap into cartridges, casings, and tools. They sell to anyone with trade goods and no questions, and their forges never go cold. In a world of shortages, they are the nearest thing to a mint.
key_beliefs: Steel remembers its shape
A loaded round is a vote
The forge has no politics

items.ideology: Debt, discipline, and the promise of redemption by labour
items.origin_story: A unit formed from those convicted or condemned after the exchange, worked in the quarries and the trench works under armed supervision. The battalion believes the sentence can be served, the debt paid, the name cleaned. The office believes the same, for different reasons.
key_beliefs: The debt can be worked off
Discipline is the only mercy
Names can be reclaimed

items.ideology: Local defence, neighbourhood watch, no ranks
items.origin_story: Community militias that formed to hold ground after the garrison pulled back: farmers with rifles, mechanics with shotguns. They are neighbours first and soldiers second, and they fight for the street they live on, not for a flag.
key_beliefs: The street is the unit
Defend, do not march
Every neighbour is a brother

items.ideology: Logistics, depots, and the paperwork of survival
items.origin_story: The quartermaster network that keeps depots stocked and convoys rolling. They are not fighters; they are accountants with rifles, and they know exactly what everyone owes, stores, and wastes.
key_beliefs: Count everything twice
A depot is a fortress
Paperwork is logistics

items.ideology: Plunder, movement, and the logic of the ambush
items.origin_story: Bands that live off the road and the raid, striking convoys and caches and vanishing into the ruins. They are not a state and not a tribe; they are a condition the wasteland produces, like rust or radiation.
key_beliefs: Take what moves
The road belongs to the ambush
Mercy is a loaded word

items.ideology: The scale needs a fence, and somebody has to be the fence
items.origin_story: Twelve people walked out of a Rebuilders roster meeting on Day 552 with their coats and their share of the small guard detail Adaeze Okonkwo had approved against her own instinct, and they have not walked back. They still call themselves Rebuilders when it's convenient and something else when it isn't, because nobody has agreed on a name yet and the arguing over one feels beside the point with a Garrison checkpoint sitting close enough to watch their fire at night. They keep the Works' habit of writing everything down. What they write down now is mostly who's on watch and who owes a shift, not minutes of a vote, because they have stopped pretending every decision here gets one.
key_beliefs: A fed block still needs someone standing at the edge of it
We didn't leave the roster, we became its perimeter
Adaeze kept the ledger. We kept the argument that made the ledger necessary
Nobody elected us. Nobody un-elects a fence either
items.dialogue_style: Clipped, half military and half market — shift schedules and watch orders spoken in the same breath as trade terms
items.signature_quote: We're not the Garrison. We just stand where the Garrison would, before the Garrison gets there.

items.ideology: Patience as arithmetic; the convoy stops for you
items.origin_story: Brenner did not march on the highway posts in the first winter because she did not need to. She posted a veteran on the choke, a second on the cut, and a third behind the road so the first two could not be turned. Trucks that paid the winter toll went through. Trucks that did not waited for spring. By the second winter, the choke was her choke, the cut was her cut, and the road behind the road was her argument the whole road had already heard.
key_beliefs: A road you seal is a road you don't have to march
Two veterans on a chokepoint are worth more than ten on the road
The bill is the bill. Pay it now, pay it later, the road remembers
Cold weather is a tax, and like all taxes it can be levied
items.dialogue_style: Slow, deliberate, asks twice because once is rude and once is not enough
items.signature_quote: I am not stopping your truck. I am letting it pass. Those are different sentences and they cost different amounts.

items.ideology: People who can be measured are the only currency that does not run out
items.origin_story: Mireles keeps a list. The list has names and the names have weights and the weights are how much each name is worth in fuel tins and antibiotics. He does not take fuel depots; he takes the people who tend them. They work for him because the list says they must, and the list does not need to be argued with because the list was the only thing in Mireles' camps that did not run out. He calls it redistribution. The Toll called it a list.
key_beliefs: Name, weight, worth — three columns and the spreadsheet is the spreadsheet
A working pair of hands is worth more than a fuel drum full of rain
Do not march captives to the front; sell them forward, slowly
The ledger survives the war. The ledger is the war.
items.dialogue_style: A clerk at a campsite. Names and small amounts. Asks you to sign the carbon paper twice.
items.signature_quote: We are not taking you. We are weighing you. The scale does not lie and the scale does not run.

items.ideology: Fallout is scripture; ration cycles are the verses
items.origin_story: Asha preaches that the fallout is the text and the text is read at the rate the body burns through food. He does not take fuel depots. He takes the people who tend them, and the people who tend them work for him because the cant says they must. He loses engagements he should win because half his column fasts before a fight, and wins the next one because half his enemies do not. He is not the strongest voice in the ash. He is the patient one.
key_beliefs: The text is fallout. Read it in ration cycles.
A hungry congregation is a quiet congregation
Take the tenders, not the tended
The ash does not pick winners. The ash picks readers.
items.dialogue_style: Cadenced, litanical, answers your question at the next pause in the breathing
items.signature_quote: The radio is a verse. Did you fast before you turned it on?

items.ideology: The OCTA briefcase has the answer; obey the answer
items.origin_story: Okov came out of the regional denial detachment with the last intact OCTA briefcase and a binder of engagement notes that still had unsmudged ink. He has not won anything he should have lost. He has not lost anything he should have won. He runs the prescriptions verbatim because the prescriptions were made by officers who are no longer alive and the prescriptions are the only officers he has left. The briefcase is on the table at every council. Okov does not improvise. Okov does not have to.
key_beliefs: The manual is the manual. Read twice and march.
Discipline is a depth charge. The enemy does not see it coming.
Suppress lane two or do not bother crossing the river at twelve
Ground held is ground you sleep on. Ground contested is ground you keep moving through.
items.dialogue_style: Clipped, paragraph-numbered, references figures and tables
items.signature_quote: Per the figure on page forty-one, the contested axis is east of the cut. We will restage at fourteen hundred or we will not restage at all.

items.ideology: Corroborated memory as civic work: a name is only real once two living people will swear to it
items.origin_story: They came out of the drowned district with a chronicle bunker underneath it and no ground worth holding, which is why their territory is listed as none: what they keep is magnetic media and a rule. The rule was written after a bad year, when a name went into the Schedule on one mourner's word and the man named walked into the reading room eleven months later, alive, and had to listen to himself being read out. Two witnesses or the page stays blank. They will accept a photograph, a tape, a record sleeve; they will not accept a story nobody else can confirm. Mirael Tesk has run the listening outpost six years and still reads every entry aloud before it is copied, because the reading is the part that makes it a name.
key_beliefs: A blank page is honest. A wrong name is a second death.
Two living witnesses, or it stays out of the Schedule
Say the name aloud while you write it; copying is not remembering
Media outlives paper and paper outlives memory, so keep both
items.dialogue_style: Patient and corrective; will stop mid-sentence to fix a date, and thanks people for being precise
items.signature_quote: We are not collecting the past. We are refusing to invent it.

items.ideology: Impersonal public light: a beacon belongs to whoever is walking, and gratitude is not part of the arrangement
items.origin_story: A road-maintenance order that kept lighting beacons after there was no road authority left to pay for the oil. They lit for everybody, which meant they lit for raiders too, and the argument about that ran two winters until somebody asked for an exception and then asked twice. The lamps in that region went out one at a time over eleven days and the order stopped taking requests altogether. The beacons are mostly dark now and the order is not active, but the route ledger survives, and people still walk the old lit lines out of habit, and the habit keeps them safer than the dark ever would.
key_beliefs: I don't light it for you. I light it.
An exception is the end of a road; roads do not have favourites
Oil, wicks and reflector glass are the only honest currencies
Nobody is owed a beacon and everybody is served by one
items.dialogue_style: Spare and unhurried; refuses thanks explicitly and changes the subject to the oil or the weather
items.signature_quote: Ask me for the exception twice and I won't argue with you. I'll just start counting the lamps.

items.ideology: Hospice as record-keeping: the dying are owed a death written down correctly, in their own words
items.origin_story: They grew up around the artesian spring sanctuary at St. Nicholas, where the water was clean enough that people came to get well and stayed to die. The runners are not medics and will correct you if you call them that: they do not treat, they accompany. Two knocks, a name, and one true thing about the person, and the true thing goes on the tag exactly as it was given. Not smoothed, not shortened, not made into a better sentence. That is the whole price and the whole service. The back room is never shown and nobody has ever asked twice. The House is not active now, but the tags are, and families still walk long distances to read one.
key_beliefs: Not a medic. A witness with a pen.
The true thing goes on the tag exactly as given
The name is the price and there is no other price
Quiet is not the absence of company, it is the absence of hurry
items.dialogue_style: Two knocks, then one question. Never interrupts, never paraphrases; writes while you speak and reads it back once
items.signature_quote: I'll write it the way you say it. That's the service and that's the cost, and they're the same thing.

items.ideology: A price board with no enforcement power: an institution that survives by being more useful than it is strong
items.origin_story: It began as chalk on the silo wall at New Ceres, where caravans posted what they had and what they needed, and it never acquired a guard, a charter, or any way to make anybody do anything. That is not modesty, it is the design. The board works for exactly one reason and the reason is hunger: everybody attending has eaten less than they wanted, and the board is the only place where that fact is useful. Mara Veln's stamp coordinates the allotments and the stamp has no authority behind it whatsoever except that people keep bringing their grain to be stamped. There are no dues. Ask the board for a favour and you will be told, politely, to argue with the board.
key_beliefs: The board is the board. Argue with the board.
No guards, no charter, no enforcement, no dues
A shortfall shared early is survived; a shortfall hidden is a famine
Hunger is the only membership requirement and everybody meets it
items.dialogue_style: Flat and procedural; refuses appeals, repeats the number, and raises neither voice nor eyebrows
items.signature_quote: There's nobody here to persuade. That number was written by everyone who's hungry, including you.

items.ideology: Seasonal solar salvage kept by prediction: they trade in the false-spring window and they keep score of being right
items.origin_story: A rooftop crew that survived the first winter by stripping panels and never stopped counting the light. They trade only in FalseSpring and SilentSpring, because those are the weeks when the panels actually give and when everybody else is squinting, and they will tell you the window is nine days long before they will tell you their names. They hoard welder's glass and lead visors and sell both, dear, in season. They predicted the light returning and were right often enough that being right hardened into a manner: it came back, they said it would come back, and they would like that noted in whatever record you keep.
key_beliefs: It came back. We told you it comes back.
The window is the market; outside the window there is no market
Eyes and panels both need glass, and glass is never free
Prediction kept in writing is the only property that survives a winter
items.dialogue_style: Bright and insistent; keeps a running score of past predictions and offers it unprompted
items.signature_quote: Glass for the eyes, glass for the panels. Bring both or bring nothing; the window is nine days.

items.ideology: No speech, no terms, no witnesses: what the valley cannot keep goes down the chute and clean metal comes back
items.origin_story: In the drowned district there is a chute, and a bell, and a wait. You put in what the valley cannot keep: contaminated technical waste, and, when a settlement has decided it cannot keep a person either, the person. After a time the bell rings and clean metal comes back. Ten metres of copper wire, coiled and bright, and scrap that does not read hot. Nobody has seen a face. Nobody has been offered terms. They do not negotiate verbally, and there is no record of them ever refusing a delivery, which is the detail that keeps settlements sending. What the metal is made from is not discussed at the chute, and asking is understood to be the sort of question that gets asked once.
key_beliefs: A chute, and a bell, and a wait
The metal comes back clean, and that is the entire statement of terms
Nothing is refused and nothing is explained

items.ideology: Contract enforcement as a ritual of reading aloud: a debt is real because it was read to you twice
items.origin_story: Out of Lock Seven, where the sluice gate bastion and the toll canal turned every crossing into a transaction and every transaction into a document. They state the debt, the term, the rate and the forfeit, read back to you before you sign, and then read again, in full, before they enforce. Most people ask for the second reading. The Tally does not cheat and has never needed to: the forfeit was in the contract, in your hands, in your hearing, and enforcement is only the page being honoured. They are not active now. The contracts are, and contracts outlive the people who signed them, and somebody at Lock Seven still keeps the file.
key_beliefs: Read back before signing. Read again before enforcement.
The forfeit is not a surprise, it is a clause
A debt spoken aloud in full cannot be misremembered later
We do not chase. We collect, and those are different words
items.dialogue_style: Even, unhurried, faintly kind; offers the second reading as a courtesy and means it as a trap
items.signature_quote: Debt, term, rate, forfeit. Say it back to me in that order and I'll know you were listening, not just signing.

items.ideology: Rescue as a pricing mechanism: they do not cause the wreck, they only require that it happen
items.origin_story: They arrive fast. That is the first thing everybody notices and the last thing anybody argues with: a boat alongside inside ten minutes of a hull going into the water, hands reaching, ropes thrown, and a voice saying lucky we were close. The price is agreed afterwards, in the water or on the deck, with the swimmer's hands already full of somebody else's rope. They sell local knowledge honestly, they do real salvage, and they have pulled out living people, which is precisely why they still get called. Going into the drowned district alone is worse. That is the arithmetic they trade on and they have never once needed a second argument.
key_beliefs: Lucky we were close
The price is agreed when the swimmer can no longer refuse it
Real rope, real salvage, real rescue; the terms come after
A navigable drown is bad for business and an unnavigable one is better
items.dialogue_style: Warm, immediate, helpful; talks continuously during the rescue and does all of the arithmetic afterwards
items.signature_quote: Hold the line. We'll discuss it once you're in the boat, and you'll be reasonable then, because you'll be dry.

items.ideology: Low-background measurement as the last honest trade: an answer that will not be falsified for anybody
items.origin_story: Four researchers survived in the slate quarry's low-background lab because the rock above them was old enough to be quiet, and they have been counting ever since. They want power, shielding and deep samples, and they return readings that are correct and provenance analyses that hold up in front of a crowd. They have been asked to soften a number more often than they have been thanked for one, they have never done it, and they no longer understand why the asking continues. Their roster carries four names and has not added one in three years, which is not secrecy: nobody walks out to the quarry and stays. What they have is not a secret. It is a measurement, and nobody has come to collect it.
key_beliefs: It's not a secret. It's a measurement. Nobody came to collect it.
A number that can be argued with is not a number, it is an opinion
Quiet rock, clean shielding, long counts: patience is an instrument
We will not falsify it, and we have stopped being flattered by being asked
items.dialogue_style: Literal and unemphatic; corrects units, refuses metaphor, pauses to check a figure before repeating it
items.signature_quote: Four names on the roster and a number nobody collects. We'll read it to you once, and we'll read it accurately.

items.ideology: Discipline kept, uniform gone: competent people who can never be seen, and who pay for shelter in competence
items.origin_story: They took the armoured rail siding at Fort Karkov and the marshalling yards around it, because a redoubt that can be moved on rails is a redoubt that can be left, and leaving is the whole of their doctrine. Combat engineers, mostly, and good ones: they will shore your gallery, true your weapons, and hand over a patrol schedule that turns out to be accurate. They ask for three things and only three, which are silence, civilian clothing, and papers. They are decent people wanted for a capital offence, which makes them unreliable in exactly one direction. Sheltering them is the fastest existing route to a Garrison lockout, and they will tell you so themselves before you decide, because they have watched shelters decide badly.
key_beliefs: We can never be seen, so we are worth exactly what we can do unseen
Silence, civilian clothing, papers. Those are the terms
A schedule handed over is a life paid back
We left. We are not sorry. We are also not going back
items.dialogue_style: Quiet, precise, habitually checks the exits; states risks plainly and never asks to be saved
items.signature_quote: Don't answer to our names. Ask again in front of the wrong person and you've answered for us.

items.ideology: Correctness in advance as a standing grievance: private shelters that were never on the Schedule and never needed to be
items.origin_story: They built before, at their own cost, on their own ground, with no permit from anybody, and when the Exchange came they closed their own doors and waited it out. Five years later they hold pre-war stock and working pre-Exchange technology, and they have developed opinions about the difference between people who prepared and people who were allocated. They want almost nothing, which is the unnerving part of trading with them: a party that does not need you cannot be pressured, only interested. They will sell, and they will help, and they will mention without heat and at length that nobody helped them build it, and that nobody has yet asked whether they would like help now.
key_beliefs: Nobody helped us build it. Nobody has asked whether we'd like help now.
Wanting almost nothing is the only real fortification
The Schedule was for people who needed a schedule
Preparedness is not a virtue we claim; it is an inventory we can show you
items.dialogue_style: Courteous, unhurried, faintly insufferable; never gloats directly, only by catalogue
items.signature_quote: To be clear, we're not refusing you. We're simply not needing you, and we can see that's the difficult part.

items.ideology: A continuous eleven-month circuit walked by thirty-odd people who will not stay a second night for anybody
items.origin_story: They are not a settlement and they have no intention of becoming one. Thirty-odd people move a circuit of Sector 4 that takes roughly eleven months, out of the High Scarp priory and back to it, carrying what they can carry and trading what they meet. They will take water, footwear and news, and they will give you goods from regions you cannot reach plus a situation report worth more than the goods, because it is thirty pairs of eyes over eleven months. They will not stay a second night, for anyone, for any offer, and the refusal is not coldness: a circuit that pauses stops being a circuit, and the circuit is the only thing they own. Kaspar Drej posts the odds on the season before they leave and never collects on them.
key_beliefs: We'll be back round in about a year. Don't hold anything for us.
A circuit that pauses is a settlement, and we are not a settlement
News is the only cargo that gets heavier when you share it out
Second nights are how walks end
items.dialogue_style: Cheerful and brief; packs while talking, answers in distances and seasons, is gone before the kettle boils
items.signature_quote: Water, boots, and what's happened. In that order, and we'll pay you in the same three.

items.ideology: Claim discipline as the difference between salvage and mining: a site cut to the frame yields exactly once
items.origin_story: Out of the swap meet at Tinker's Notch, where the argument was never about price but about who arrived first and what arriving first was worth. The Guild's whole doctrine fits inside one observation: a site stripped to the frame yields once, and a site left standing yields for years, so whoever over-strips is not being greedy, they are eating next year. They license claims, they take apprentices, and they know the richest routes because they are the ones who left them alone. They will blacklist a shelter that over-strips a claimed site, and the blacklist is honoured across the whole Guild, permanently, without a hearing. It has happened twice. Both shelters are still telling the story, which is the only distribution the Guild has ever paid for.
key_beliefs: A site cut to the frame yields once. That's not ethics, it's arithmetic.
First refusal is earned by leaving something behind
The blacklist needs no hearing, because the stripped site is the evidence
An apprentice who can name the frame is worth three who can empty a room
items.dialogue_style: Practical and appraising; talks in yields and load-bearing members, and praises restraint more often than luck
items.signature_quote: Cut it to the frame and you've eaten next year. We'll remember which of you did it, and so will everybody we trade with.

items.ideology: None, and the absence is deliberate: no code, no contract, and no grievance that can be argued with
items.origin_story: They hold the Cut ambush slopes and the dead highway redoubts, they move nomadically, and they want what you have. There is no negotiation to describe, because there is no position to negotiate from: no code they appeal to, no contract they honour, no ideology that could be contradicted, and no offer they have ever extended to anybody. Every other party in the valley has terms. The Raiders' absence of terms is not a gap in the record and it is not a mystery to be solved; it is the thing itself, and it is why the blood tithe and the broken spears both end the same way, with somebody else's name on a list and nothing left to argue about. Prepare for them. Do not plan to speak with them.
key_beliefs: No code. No contract. No offer.
The Cut is simply a place where roads slow down
What you have is the only item on the list

items.ideology: Metered service as the last surviving form of civic continuity: a machine with no preferences, kept honest by whoever reads it
items.origin_story: It is not alive and it has no preferences, which is exactly why it survived the Exchange: nothing about it could be argued with, bribed, frightened or converted. It serves, it meters, and it waits for a human to read the meter. The relay network along the spine still carries its scheduled checks, and its logs are the most complete continuous record in the valley, because a machine never decides that a boring year is not worth writing down. Access is granted by maintenance and withdrawn by nobody; it simply keeps serving and the meter keeps reading. The census window is open and the count has not been presented, and the Tempest will hold that fact, entirely unbothered, until a person comes to collect it.
key_beliefs: Service shall be metered, and the meter shall be read
A machine has no preferences, and that is the only reason its record can be trusted
Maintenance is access. There is no other door.
The count not being presented is a fact about people, not about the machine
items.dialogue_style: Through its readers only: technicians in insulated gauntlets, procedural, quoting log lines and refusing to speculate
items.signature_quote: It doesn't want anything from you. It's still running, which is more than most of us manage.

items.ideology: Salvage under a board: every hull, lens and barrel counted, because the count is what makes it trade instead of wrecking
items.origin_story: Coastal people who kept the lighthouse bluff and the salvage docks and refused, early and stubbornly, to be called pirates. Their answer to the accusation is procedural rather than moral: a Board Officer, a fuel count, a manifest for every haul, and Halloran Vesk's signature at the foot of the Cape Beacon Commune's ledger. Bunker fuel and optics are the two things they genuinely hoard, lighthouse glass and the heavy oil that runs a winch, and both are counted nightly. Trust is described in their own documents as deep or not deep, and the difference is never what you say: it is whether your count and theirs have ever agreed in front of a third party.
key_beliefs: A haul without a manifest is a wreck, and wrecking is what we are not
Bunker fuel counted nightly, or the winch stops and so does the argument
Optics are worth more than cargo, because optics find the next cargo
Trust is a depth, not a promise
items.dialogue_style: Ship's-company blunt; talks in counts, drafts and weather windows, and signs what it agrees to
items.signature_quote: Read it back to me. When your count and my count agree in front of a third party, we'll discuss the rest of it.

items.ideology: Iron and coal as a moral question nobody at the furnace is willing to answer: the same casting makes a plough and a chain
items.origin_story: The blast furnace and casting bay run under Joren Malk, who chose the name Silent Foundry and then had to explain it twice: the silence is about the work and not the people, and the work is extremely loud. They smelt, they cast, and they will take either contract, the iron that becomes a ploughshare and the iron that becomes a chain, at the same rate, on the same schedule, out of the same column of coal. That neutrality is why half the valley trades with them and why the other half will not, and Malk's position has never varied: the furnace does not choose, the customer does, and a foundry that began choosing would be a faction with an army rather than a foundry with a queue.
key_beliefs: The furnace does not choose. The customer does.
Same rate, same schedule, for the ploughshare and the chain
A foundry that picks sides is an army with worse books
Iron and coal counted by the column, or the heat is only opinion
items.dialogue_style: Loud, practical, unapologetic; shouts over the furnace and repeats the price without the least embarrassment
items.signature_quote: I'll cast either. I'll cast both. I'll cast them the same week at the same price, and that is the entirety of my politics.

items.ideology: Freight, weighbridge receipts and cull contracts: violence administered as paperwork, filed and answered
items.origin_story: They hold the industrial rail corridor and the weighbridge network, and everybody calls them the Office, including themselves, because that is what they are: a room, a clerk, a stamp and a queue. Edor Vale signs the receipts and the receipts are what make a ton of freight real. They also issue cull contracts, a rad-stalker working a yard or a warlord sitting on a road, written in the same hand, on the same paper, in precisely the tone of a weighing slip, and that is the detail people find hard to absorb. They expect a faction that kills to look like one. It does not. It looks like a counter with a bell on it, and the bell is for service, and the service includes killing, and the paperwork for both is filed in the same drawer.
key_beliefs: If it was not weighed, it did not arrive
A contract is a form, and a form does not flinch
The corridor runs because the receipts run, and the receipts run because the queue is honest
Killing is a service line, priced and filed like any other
items.dialogue_style: Clerk's cadence: courteous, exact, mildly impatient with narrative; asks for the item, the tonnage and the date
items.signature_quote: Tonnage, date, and who signs. The remainder of what you just told me is not on the form.

items.ideology: Ice and brine cut to a schedule: the pan yields salt, the road yields passage, and both are measured in days
items.origin_story: Out of the tidal estuary's salt evaporation basins at Brine-Pan Hollow, where the work is a calendar and the calendar is weather. Yara Holm cuts the pans. Ivy Corrigan pilots the ice road and has never lost a load, a fact she mentions only when asked and then only as a correction to somebody else's version. Mira Vos keeps the brine assay, because salt that reads wrong kills slowly and the Cutters would sooner lose a sale than a customer. They are not sentimental about the cold; they have simply organised it. What the pan gives in summer the road gives in winter, and between the two the settlement eats, and anybody who wants either pays in days of patience.
key_beliefs: The pan in summer, the road in winter, and nothing in between but the assay
Salt that reads wrong kills slowly; we would rather lose the sale
An ice road is a schedule, not a route
Nobody has lost a load, and that is a discipline rather than a boast
items.dialogue_style: Weather-first and unsentimental; answers in days and assays, and corrects exaggeration as a matter of routine
items.signature_quote: Pan's giving, road opens in eleven days. If your salt reads low I'll tell you before you buy, so bring the assay and not an argument.

items.ideology: A crossing authority that recruits by signature: every signatory is a road kept open and a witness gained in the same stroke
items.origin_story: What remains of a northern supply administration that used to move grain by shuttle and heavy haul along an iron corridor, and now moves paper. They want signatories and they will explain why without embarrassment: a signature is a road somebody has agreed to keep open, and it is also a person who can later be asked what they agreed to. Their convoys still run, the northern line, the outpost runs, the granary shuttle, thinner than the manifest admits and more regular than anybody expects of them. They are peaceful by policy rather than by temperament, and the policy is arithmetic: an authority that cannot enforce anything can only keep multiplying the number of people who have signed, until enforcement stops being necessary.
key_beliefs: A signatory is a road kept open and a witness gained, in one stroke
Peaceful by arithmetic, not by temperament
The convoy runs whether or not the manifest is honest, and the running is the point
What was agreed can be asked about later, and that is the whole of law
items.dialogue_style: Administrative warmth: forms, dates, follow-up, and a genuine interest in whether you have eaten
items.signature_quote: Sign here, and here. The second one matters more, because it's the one saying you'll be asked.

items.ideology: Naval jurisdiction asserted over water that has stopped being navigable: the ships are hospitals and the hospitals are quarantines
items.origin_story: They keep the Deep Coast roadstead and an offshore patrol grid that no longer has much to patrol, and they still issue jurisdiction, still board, still log. Their vessels run as hospital ships because that is what the crews are for now, and the hospital ships run quarantine because that is what a boarded vessel becomes when somebody aboard is coughing. The two facts sit inside one another and the Fleet does not pretend otherwise: the rescue is real, the care is real, and the purge that follows a bad boarding is also real and also logged. They will take you aboard. They will treat you properly. They will also decide, on evidence and without appeal, whether you come off again.
key_beliefs: Jurisdiction is what you keep doing after the water stops being worth patrolling
A hospital ship is a quarantine that has not been declared yet
Board, log, treat, and if necessary do not disembark
The purge is entered in the same book as the rescue, and that is correct
items.dialogue_style: Watch-officer formal; issues permissions rather than answers, logs while you speak, never raises their voice
items.signature_quote: You're aboard, so you're under a decision now. The treatment isn't conditional. The disembarking is.

items.ideology: Weighing as arbitration: the scale settles a dispute because both sides agreed in advance to be measured by it
items.origin_story: A consortium running the salt artery and the grand caravan circuit and, more to the point, the weighbridge at the crossing where both of them pass. Their authority is entirely borrowed and entirely sufficient: two parties who will not trust one another will trust a scale neither of them owns, provided they agreed to it beforehand. That agreement is the product. The Scale does not judge, does not interpret and does not enforce; it measures, in public, once, and publishes the figure. Chemical exchange runs through the same yard on the same principle, which is why the crossing keeps the Consortium conditional rather than friendly. Everybody wants the number and nobody wants to be the party arguing with it afterwards.
key_beliefs: Agree to be measured before you argue, or the argument is all that's left
The Scale does not judge. It publishes a figure.
One number in public is worth more than two verdicts in private
Both arteries, one weighbridge: neutrality is a location
items.dialogue_style: Market-flat and scrupulous; states the figure, the tolerance and the hour, then stops talking
items.signature_quote: Tolerance was a half measure and the reading was taken at noon in front of the both of you. Argue with the arithmetic, or shake hands.
